papers.title: Sleep Homeostasis Has Circaseptan and Circatrigintan Cycles Over Year-Long Timescales.
papers.abstract: Sleep homeostasis, the process by which sleep pressure accumulated during wakefulness is dissipated across non-rapid eye movement (REM) sleep, can be quantified as the nightly rate of decline in slow-wave activity (SWA; 0.5-4 Hz). Disruption of this homeostatic process has been documented in a range of neurological disorders including epilepsy, Alzheimer's disease and REM sleep behaviour disorder, yet its long-term dynamics in healthy individuals remain uncharacterized. The advent of subscalp EEG (sqEEG) platforms now makes continuous, naturalistic sleep recording feasible over months, enabling longitudinal study of sleep homeostasis at an unprecedented scale. Here we report the first such characterization in 20 healthy adults recorded continuously over 12-15 months. SWA slope was predominantly negative across all subjects, confirming intact homeostatic regulation and was stable across sex and age. Continuous wavelet transform analysis revealed significant circaseptan (~7-day) and circatrigintan (~28-day) rhythmicity in the majority of subjects, independent of sex. These findings establish a normative baseline for long-term sleep homeostatic dynamics and suggest that homeostatic sleep pressure dissipation is organized across multiple timescales beyond the single night, with direct relevance for neurological conditions in which this process is disrupted.

papers.title: DPYD links glial lipids and myelination to sleep duration
papers.abstract: The regulation of sleep is heritable and conserved across species1,2, but the governing genetic mechanisms remain poorly understood. Here, we investigate the role of DPYD--which encodes the pyrimidine catabolic enzyme, dihydropyrimidine dehydrogenase--in sleep. Using a cross-species approach, we show that DPYD and its orthologs act specifically in glia to promote sleep through the regulation of brain lipids. In mouse and zebrafish, we find that DPYD orthologs are enriched in oligodendrocyte lineage cells, and their loss reduces myelination and sleep independent of DPYDs established role in uracil catabolism to {beta}-alanine. Genetic and pharmacological manipulations of myelin in zebrafish show that altering myelination is sufficient to perturb sleep duration. In Drosophila, which lack myelin, we find that the DPYD ortholog acts in ensheathing glia to promote sleep through formation of glial lipid droplets, a proposed evolutionary precursor to myelin. Furthermore, a human GWAS-identified sleep variant2 resides in a conserved cis-regulatory element that selectively contacts the promoter of DPYD within oligodendrocytes, connecting the human genetic association to oligodendrocyte-specific control of DPYD. Together, these results identify a deeply conserved role for glial lipids in sleep regulation and establish DPYD as a mechanistic link between myelin biology and sleep.

papers.title: Standard touchscreen test procedures shift circadian rhythms in mice: a modified protocol to minimize circadian confounds
papers.abstract: Touchscreen based cognitive testing for rodents offers considerable experimental benefits, including a semi automated battery approach and the use of appetitive rather than aversive reinforcement. However, food reward and touchscreen illumination introduce potential confounds, as both food and light can shift, entrain, or disrupt circadian rhythms, which in turn can affect learning and memory. The potential for the test apparatus to impact endogenous circadian rhythms is particularly problematic when probing relationships between sleep, circadian disruption, and cognitive performance. After observing phase shifting of circadian rhythms in nocturnal mice tested using standard touchscreen test procedures, which include testing during the active period (early lights off), we evaluated the relative contributions of the illuminated screen and the appetitive food reward. Our results indicate that light emitted by the touchscreen chambers is responsible for the circadian phase shifting effects, with standard screen conditions inducing a ~3.5 h phase delay in daily activity rhythms when training is conducted early in the dark period for 7 consecutive days. We then modified lighting in the test environment and the home cage to identify parameters that would minimize circadian shifting without impairing visual discrimination or performance on a widely used cognitive test (Trial Unique Nonmatching to Location, TUNL). From the 10 conditions tested, we offer specific recommendations for modifying touchscreen test protocols to minimize circadian confounds, without impacting task acquisition or performance.

papers.title: Closed-loop acoustic stimulation promotes local slow oscillation train initiation and persistence in elderly adults
papers.abstract: Slow oscillations (SOs) during non-rapid eye movement (NREM) sleep support memory consolidation and metabolic waste clearance. Aging is associated with reduced SO amplitude and density and disrupted temporal organization, characterized by more isolated events and shorter SO trains. We investigated whether closed-loop acoustic stimulation (CLAS) could enhance the initiation and persistence of rhythmic SO activity in elderly adults. Twenty-seven participants underwent a baseline night followed by an experimental night, during which online-detected SOs were either stimulated using CLAS (STIM; n = 16) or left unstimulated (SHAM; n = 11). We quantified the proportions of isolated and consecutive SOs, train-initiation probability, and SO train length. Analyses assessed local effects around online-detected SOs and global effects across NREM sleep using offline detection. Locally, CLAS reduced the proportion of isolated SOs and increased the proportion of consecutive SOs, train-initiation probability, and mean train length. Global overnight effects were weaker but directionally consistent, primarily reflecting a shift toward longer SO trains. These changes occurred without a significant between-group difference in the change in SO density, and local effects remained significant after adjustment for SO density. Thus, CLAS promoted sustained rhythmic activity beyond changes in SO occurrence. These findings suggest that CLAS can modify the temporal organization of SOs in elderly adults, supporting its potential to mitigate age-related disruptions in SO dynamics. Temporal organization measures may complement conventional amplitude and density measures when evaluating CLAS effects. Further studies should establish whether these changes translate into cognitive benefits or improvements in other aspects of brain health.

papers.title: Circadian multimodal physiological, ocular and behavioural data from a 40-hour forced-desynchrony protocol
papers.abstract: We present a multimodal dataset from twelve healthy adults (aged 19-30 years, 50% female) who completed a 40-hour ultra-short sleep-wake forced desynchrony protocol which scheduled 2 h 30 min of wakefulness in dim light and 1 h 15 min of sleep in darkness (2:1 wake:sleep ratio), with the protocol ending after the last wake period. This schedule compressed the typical 24-hour day into an ultradian 3 h 45 min cycle to decouple circadian and homeostatic influences on physiology and behaviour. During each wake interval, participants completed repeated assessments of visual psychophysics (chromatic temporal contrast sensitivity), pupillometry with silent-substitution stimuli, ocular structure (optical coherence tomography) and physiology (intraocular pressure), psychomotor vigilance, salivary hormones, and standardised questionnaires, alongside continuous actigraphy, electrocardiography, and recordings of core and peripheral temperature, blood pressure, and interstitial glucose. Two supplementary evening sessions under experimental light exposure and dim-light conditions provide comparison data on circadian phase (salivary melatonin concentration, dim-light melatonin onset). Data collected from one pilot participant and screenings of two excluded candidates are additionally included. This dataset supports reuse for investigating circadian dynamics across multiple domains beyond the retinal-function hypotheses of the original study.

papers.title: What Are Recent Insights Into Pontomedullary Circuits Controlling in REM Sleep?
papers.abstract: Recent studies have identified neurochemically defined neuronal groups in the pons and medulla that have a critical role in initiation, maintenance, and manifestations of REM sleep (REM-on neurons). The sublaterodorsal tegmental nucleus (SLD) in rodents (subcoeruleus nucleus in humans) contains a group of glutamatergic neurons that express corticotrophin-releasing hormone‑binding protein (Crhbp + neurons) that initiate REM sleep and elicit REM sleep atonia by projections to inhibitory neurons of the ventromedial medulla projecting to spinal motor neurons. A reciprocal glutamatergic excitatory loop between these SLD Crhbp + neurons and neurons in the dorsomedial medulla expressing nitric oxide synthase 1 (Nos1+ neurons) form a core circuit that initiates and maintains REM sleep. Other neurochemically defined neuronal groups in the dorsomedial medulla trigger rapid eye movements and other phasic phenomena during REM sleep. Both the ventromedial medulla and the dorsomedial medulla contain GABAergic neurons that promote REM sleep by inhibiting REM-off neurons.

It also describes projections mediating REM atonia via ventromedial medulla inhibitory neurons and separate groups triggering rapid eye movements and phasic phenomena.

papers.title: A hypothalamo-septo-hippocampal circuit for REM sleep-dependent consolidation of social memory
papers.abstract: REM sleep constitutes a critical window for memory consolidation, yet the brain circuits orchestrating this process remain incompletely defined. Here, we identify a lateral supramammillary nucleus (SuM)-medial septum (MS) projection as a REM sleep-specialized pathway essential for hippocampal memory consolidation. Fiber photometry and optrode recordings revealed that lateral SuM-MS projecting neurons were selectively active during REM sleep. REM-specific optogenetic silencing of this projection impaired consolidation of both social and contextual fear memories. Crucially, silencing of its downstream target, the MS-CA2 pathway, during REM sleep selectively disrupted social memory while sparing contextual fear memory. This functional dissection establishes a hypothalamo-septo-hippocampal circuit (lateral SuM-MS-CA2) dedicated to social memory processing, in parallel to the recently-described direct SuM-CA2 pathway. These results also position the SuM as a REM sleep-hub that routes information via parallel septal pathways to consolidate distinct memory modalities.

papers.title: The Hypothalamic Paraventricular Nucleus as an Integrative Hub of Circadian Regulation and a Therapeutic Target in Disease.
papers.abstract: Circadian rhythms are endogenous, approximately 24-hour oscillations that align physiology and behavior with the environmental light-dark cycle and support homeostasis. In mammals, the suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN) serves as the central circadian pacemaker, but its neuronal projections are restricted to a relatively small set of hypothalamic targets. The hypothalamic paraventricular nucleus (PVN) is an important downstream integrative node that receives direct and indirect temporal signals from the SCN and integrates them with metabolic, visceral, stress-related, and limbic inputs. Through functionally distinct neuroendocrine, autonomic, and central-projecting neuronal populations, the PVN contributes to the temporal regulation of hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis activity, glucose metabolism, feeding behavior, nociceptive sensitivity, and cardiovascular function. Cell-type-specific genetic and transcriptomic studies further indicate that PVN neuronal populations exhibit distinct clock-related molecular programs. Studies predominantly in nocturnal rodent models have linked disruption of PVN clocks or rhythmic output to aging-associated decline, metabolic dysfunction, altered tumor immunity, neurodegenerative disease, and pain-related phenotypes. Human post-mortem studies have reported heterogeneous PVN changes in Alzheimer's disease, but direct evidence of PVN clock or SCN-PVN circuit dysfunction in humans remains limited. This review integrates circuit-, cellular-, and molecular-level evidence for the PVN's role in circadian regulation, evaluates interventions spanning timed drug delivery, meal timing, light exposure, and PVN-focused experimental manipulation, and outlines the challenges of translating preclinical findings into clinical practice.

papers.title: Enhancing deep sleep with auditory stimulation to boost cognitive training responsiveness in people with Parkinson's disease and mild cognitive impairment: Rationale and design of the double-blind randomized controlled trial PD-CogT-Sleep
papers.abstract: Background: Cognitive training (CogT) is an established non-pharmacological intervention for people with Parkinson's disease (PD) and mild cognitive impairment (PD-MCI). However, overall effects on cognitive outcomes are small to moderate and interindividually highly heterogeneous. Sleep -especially deep sleep- could be an important determinant of CogT responsiveness in PD, and may have beneficial effects on PD pathophysiology. Therefore, the enhancement of deep sleep by phase-targeted auditory stimulation (PTAS) could strengthen the effects of CogT on cognitive symptoms and counteract disease progression. Methods: PD-CogT-Sleep is a monocentric, partly decentralized, double-blind, randomized sham-controlled trial that combines two remotely delivered non-pharmacological interventions, to assess the additive effect of PTAS on digital CogT responsiveness in people with PD-MCI. The primary outcome is executive functions; Secondary and exploratory outcomes include further cognitive functions, participant-reported outcome measures, blood-based biomarkers, and high-density sleep electroencephalography markers. Outcomes are assessed at baseline, five weeks post-allocation and at 3-month follow-up. We aim to consecutively recruit N=50 participants, who will be randomized 1:1 to receive CogT+PTAS or CogT+Sham. Discussion: The PD-CogT-Sleep study integrates wearable and digital technologies to systematically combine a novel, non-invasive, sleep-enhancing intervention (PTAS) with established CogT to improve cognition and evaluate PTAS' disease-modifying potential through its effects on blood-based biomarkers in PD-MCI. The expected results will foster our understanding of the interplay of sleep, cognition, and neurodegeneration, and may guide further development of safe, feasible, scalable, patient-centered, technology-based non-pharmacological interventions counteracting cognitive decline in neurodegenerative diseases.

papers.title: Photoentrainment as Bayesian Inference: How the central circadian clock may weight and integrate the intensity and wavelength of natural light to estimate astronomical time
papers.abstract: Synchronising with the Earth's 24-hour rotation using natural light as a timing cue presents a problem for the mammalian brain's central circadian clock. Natural light is highly variable and can take a range of values at any given time of day. For example, it fluctuates due to differences in weather conditions and across seasons. Therefore, an absolute value of light provides an uncertain indication of the time of day. Despite this uncertainty, the central clock maintains close alignment with astronomical time, and here we describe how this may be achieved computationally. We present a Bayesian model in which the clock's endogenous oscillation is used to predict the probability of observing features of light, including intensity and spectral composition, and their co-occurrence given the time of day. These predictions are drawn from a distribution of values typically experienced. When observed light falls outside the predicted range, a prediction error provides evidence that the clock may be misaligned with astronomical time. How much the clock adjusts its phase depends on the relative uncertainty associated with its internal prediction and observed light. These are combined as a weighted average according to their relative reliability, drawing the clock's updated phase towards whichever provides the more reliable estimate of astronomical time. Using natural light measurements collected over one week from 59 human observers and 100 days of environmental spectral measurements, we characterize how the variability of natural light systematically changes across the day and show how the clock may exploit this structure for circadian timekeeping. The model explains how the canonical shape of the phase response curve emerges from the relationship between light distributions and time of day, and how properties of light, including intensity and spectral composition, can be integrated according to their reliability. The central clock's synchrony to light may represent a specific instance of a general computational strategy employed by the mammalian nervous system, whereby sensory information is interpreted relative to an internally generated prediction.

papers.title: Transient Alerting Effects of Karolinska Sleepiness Scale Ratings on Physiological and Driving Performance Indicators.
papers.abstract: The objective of this study was to determine whether subjectively rating sleepiness on the Karolinska Sleepiness Scale (KSS) gives rise to an alerting effect and, if so, how long it persists. Data from five driving simulator studies involving 83 participants were pooled. Time-locked trajectories of blink duration, blink closing velocity, heart rate, electroencephalographic (EEG) parietal α and frontal θ power, and lateral lane position variability were analysed around each KSS rating using linear mixed-effects models with condition-specific KSS baselines, a transient post-rating component, a late post-rating offset, and time-on-task terms. Immediately after the rating, several indicators shifted in an alerting direction: blink duration and standard deviation of lateral position (SDLP) decreased, blink closing velocity and heart rate increased, and parietal α power generally decreased. Frontal θ showed a more condition-dependent response. The estimated duration of the transient component was indicator dependent, ranging from 40 s for heart rate to the upper bound of the 120-s analysis window for SDLP. These findings have practical implications for driver sleepiness detection system development, validation protocols, and type-approval processes that rely on KSS as a reference measure. If ratings themselves are associated with short-lived physiological or behavioural changes, the timing and modality of KSS administration become important for ensuring valid ground truth labels. Future studies with control conditions, randomized or jittered rating times, and real-road data are needed to determine whether the rating-associated changes are causal and generalisable.

papers.title: Beyond Classification Accuracy: Building Trustworthy Artificial Intelligence for Clinical Electroencephalography.
papers.abstract: Electroencephalography (EEG) remains important in clinical neuroscience because it records brain activity as a time-resolved physiological process. It offers millisecond temporal resolution, can be used at the bedside and supports prolonged monitoring. Artificial intelligence (AI) has expanded EEG analysis through automated pattern recognition, representation learning, large-scale screening and decision support in epilepsy, sleep medicine, cognitive disorders, psychiatric conditions, intensive care, disorders of consciousness and anaesthesia monitoring. High classification accuracy in a research dataset, however, is not clinical readiness. EEG signals are shaped by physiological state, artefacts, acquisition systems, preprocessing choices and clinical context. Labels may come from expert annotations, diagnostic categories, behavioural scales, treatment responses or long-term outcomes, and these sources do not always define the same biological target. This review argues that EEG-AI translation should be judged by the strength of its evidence, not by technical performance alone. We examine why EEG is valuable yet hard to standardize, how EEG features can serve as candidate biomarkers, and why translational maturity differs across clinical scenarios. We then discuss the evidence gaps behind high-performing models, focusing on target validity, data leakage, confounding, external validation and clinically aligned metrics. Finally, we argue for clinical understandability rather than model interpretability alone, and for human-machine workflows rather than isolated classifiers. Future EEG-AI systems should be assessed by whether their outputs are biologically plausible, externally generalizable, understandable to clinicians and safe in real-world care.

It advocates for biologically plausible, externally generalizable, clinician-understandable systems evaluated in human-machine workflows.

papers.title: Circadian feeding rhythm loss drives sex-specific β-cell dysfunction in diet-induced obesity
papers.abstract: Diet-induced obesity (DIO), modeled by a high-fat diet (HFD), adversely affects circadian glucose homeostasis partly by dysregulating fasting/feeding cycles. However, its impact on circadian {beta}-cell function and relevant transcriptional programs remains unclear. To investigate this, we exposed male and female C57BL/6 mice to either chow or HFD for eight weeks and assessed behavioral (feeding/activity), physiological (glucose tolerance/insulin secretion), transcriptomic (RNA sequencing (RNA-seq)), and epigenomic (Assay for Transposase-Accessible Chromatin using Sequencing (ATAC-seq)) circadian rhythms. Additionally, we tested whether normalizing fasting/feeding cycles via time-restricted feeding (tRF) during the dark- or light-phase of the circadian cycle could mitigate DIO's deleterious effects. DIO disrupted circadian fasting/feeding rhythms, with greater disruption in males than females (p<0.05 vs. CHOW). In males, DIO abolished circadian regulation of glucose tolerance and in vivo glucose-stimulated insulin secretion (GSIS) (p<0.05 vs. chow), whereas female mice maintained circadian glucose homeostasis. RNA-seq analysis of male islets revealed a 42.1% reduction in circadian-regulated transcripts under DIO, with weakened rhythms in key {beta}-cell pathways such as insulin secretion. Moreover, ATAC-Seq analysis indicated reduced chromatin accessibility of genes/pathways related to insulin secretion and glucose hemostasis under DIO (p<0.05 vs. chow) during both dark- or light-phase of the circadian cycle. Notably, dark-phase time-restricted feeding (tRF) restored circadian glucose tolerance, GSIS, and islet gene expression, whereas light-phase tRF enhanced {beta}-cell function during the normally inactive/light phase of the circadian cycle, further suppressing circadian rhythmicity of the islet transcriptome. Motif analysis indicated that DIO suppressed the activity of D-box transcription factors (TFs) (DBP and TEF) while enhancing the activity of ETS family TFs (ELK1, ETS2, ELF2, and GABPA), which was partly mitigated by dark-phase tRF. Our study demonstrates that DIO disrupts circadian {beta}-cell function and gene expression by dysregulating fasting/feeding cycles in male mice and reveals significant sex differences in how DIO affects circadian glucose homeostasis and {beta}-cell function.

papers.title: Triphasic waves in leptomeningeal metastases and cycling alternating pattern of encephalopathy during sleep.
papers.abstract: Triphasic waves (TWs), now termed generalized periodic discharges with triphasic morphology, may be mistaken for nonconvulsive status epilepticus (NCSE), particularly in critically ill patients. Changes in vigilance over time can help distinguish encephalopathic patterns from ictal activity. A 69-year-old woman with breast cancer and leptomeningeal metastases developed progressive mutism and impaired consciousness. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis showed atypical cells and markedly elevated protein, while brain MRI demonstrated bilateral sulcal hyperintensities, most prominent in the posterior regions. An EEG performed 1 week after bevacizumab and paclitaxel were discontinued showed only mild background slowing without epileptiform discharges. A repeat EEG 1 week later showed nearly continuous TWs. The discharges disappeared during spontaneous sleep and recurred periodically, consistent with a cyclic alternating pattern of encephalopathy during sleep (CAPE). In the absence of significant metabolic and toxic derangements, these features favored an encephalopathic rather than ictal pattern. Given the advanced disease and poor prognosis, care remained supportive and palliative. This case highlights the importance of interpreting TWs within their clinical context and in relation to the state of vigilance. Their disappearance at sleep onset, with periodic recurrence during sleep producing a CAPE, supports an encephalopathic rather than ictal interpretation, helping to avoid misdiagnosis of NCSE and unnecessary administration of antiseizure medications.

papers.title: Neuropeptide signaling in perioperative neurocognitive disorders: Receptor biology, mechanistic links, and a cautious prevention framework.
papers.abstract: Perioperative neurocognitive disorders (PND) encompass postoperative delirium, delayed neurocognitive recovery, and postoperative neurocognitive disorder in patients with a vulnerable brain. Neuropeptides provide a receptor-defined signaling layer that can couple tissue injury, nociception, arousal, sleep, vascular regulation, and glial responses. This review integrates clinical and translational evidence for substance P/neurokinin-1, neuropeptide Y/Y receptors, orexin-A/orexin receptors, and vasoactive intestinal peptide/pituitary adenylate cyclase-activating polypeptide pathways within the broader biology of PND. Current human evidence is strongest for perioperative risk factors, delirium phenotyping, and selected preventive bundles; direct evidence that neuropeptide pathways cause or predict PND remains limited. We therefore distinguish established associations from preclinical mechanisms and hypothesis-generating therapeutic opportunities. The proposed framework links preoperative brain-reserve assessment and medication optimization with intraoperative protection of neurovascular and circuit function and postoperative restoration of sleep, mobility, and orientation. Biomarkers and neuropeptide signatures may enrich future trials, but no validated thresholds or individual-level neuropeptide-guided treatment pathway is currently available. Progress will require receptor-resolved assays, longitudinal human sampling, external validation, and pragmatic trials that test clinical utility rather than mechanistic plausibility alone.

papers.title: How Circadian Rhythms Shape Emotional Reactivity and Regulation: A Narrative Review.
papers.abstract: Circadian rhythms exert a profound influence on human physiology and behaviour, providing temporal organisation to sleep-wake patterns, cognitive performance, and affective functioning. Increasing evidence indicates that misalignment between internal biological clocks and external environmental or social demands critically affects emotional health. This narrative review focuses on the role of circadian rhythms in shaping emotional reactivity and regulation, with particular attention to chronotype, social jet lag (SJL) and shift work. Evening chronotypes show greater vulnerability to negative affect, difficulties in emotion regulation and a higher incidence of psychiatric symptoms compared to morning types, who typically display greater emotional stability. SJL, prevalent during adolescence, has been associated with mood disturbances, anxiety and impaired regulatory capacities, with screen exposure and late-night activities acting as aggravating factors. Similarly, shift workers frequently experience circadian desynchronisation, which disrupts executive functions essential for adaptive emotion regulation and predisposes them to stress, irritability and long-term mental health problems. Although these findings underline the strong relationship between circadian misalignment and emotional dysfunction, inconsistencies in results highlight the need for methodological refinement. Future studies should combine subjective reports with physiological markers and adopt longitudinal designs to track long-term trajectories; controlled light exposure, structured sleep-wake routines and organisational policies for shift scheduling, may represent promising avenues to strengthen resilience. By elucidating the mechanisms through which circadian rhythms modulate emotions, research can contribute to improving prevention and treatment strategies for mood and anxiety disorders, ultimately enhancing psychological well-being.

papers.title: CircaVal: a gene-centric multi-omics platform for exploring circadian regulatory features.
papers.abstract: The circadian clock orchestrates daily physiological processes through coordinated regulation of clock-controlled gene expression across multiple molecular layers. However, systematic characterization of this multilayered rhythmic regulation remains challenging because relevant information is distributed across independent datasets and rhythmicity is evaluated using diverse analytical approaches. Here, we developed CircaVal, a gene-centric multi-omics platform for the integrated exploration and interpretation of circadian regulatory features in humans, mice, and baboons. To support this framework, CircaVal processes public datasets using standardized, data-type-specific pipelines, and gene rhythmicity is integrated with tissue-specific expression, cross-species orthology, functional annotations, and multi-omics regulatory features. CircaVal further introduces an integrated rhythmicity score (IRS), which combines concordance across multiple rhythm-detection methods with reproducibility across independent datasets to provide a quantitative basis for prioritizing candidate rhythmic genes. The platform enables users to examine gene rhythmicity across datasets, identify tissue-enriched rhythmic genes, compare rhythmicity across species, and explore associated regulatory features. Additional functions include interactive gene-centric exploration, genome-browser visualization, rhythmicity analysis of user-uploaded time-series data, and programmatic data access. Together, these capabilities provide an integrated framework for rhythmic gene prioritization and gene-level interpretation of circadian regulatory features across tissues, species, datasets, and omics data types. CircaVal is freely available at https://CircaVal.com.

papers.title: Adolescent environmental enrichment prevents early-life stress-induced schizophrenia-like phenotypes via restoration of CREB-BDNF-TrkB signaling.
papers.abstract: Early-life stress (ELS) is a major environmental risk factor for schizophrenia, yet effective preventive strategies targeting its neurodevelopmental consequences remain limited. Here, we show that adolescent environmental enrichment (EE) prevents the emergence of schizophrenia-like behavioral and cognitive deficits induced by maternal separation (MS), a validated ELS model. Mechanistically, MS induced oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, neuroinflammation, neuronal apoptosis, and synaptic deficits in the hippocampus, accompanied by suppression of the CREB-BDNF-TrkB (cAMP response element-binding protein-brain-derived neurotrophic factor-tropomyosin receptor kinase B) signaling. Adolescent EE robustly reversed these abnormalities and restored neuroplasticity-related signaling. Importantly, we provide evidence supporting a causal role of TrkB signaling in these protective effects within the experimental framework used here: pharmacological activation of TrkB rescued oxidative stress-induced synaptic deficits in vitro, whereas pharmacological inhibition of TrkB abolished the behavioral and cognitive benefits of EE in vivo. To establish translational relevance, we further show that TrkB levels are significantly reduced in neuron-derived exosomes (NDEs) from patients with schizophrenia, with moderate diagnostic performance (AUC = 0.784). Together, these findings support CREB-BDNF-TrkB signaling as a key mechanistic node linking ELS to schizophrenia-related phenotypes and suggest adolescent EE as a developmentally timed, non-pharmacological intervention with translational relevance within the experimental framework used here.

papers.title: Respiratory self-similarity is a sleep apnea endotype that predicts cardiovascular disease related mortality.
papers.abstract: Pathological respiratory chemoreflex activation (high loop gain) in sleep apnea may activate the carotid body and induce excessive sympathetic nerve output, and independently add to the risk of adverse outcomes. This study aims to determine whether a high loop gain of the respiratory control system during sleep, estimated by respiratory self-similarity (SS) and the algorithm-derived central respiratory event index (CREI), is associated with new-onset cardiovascular disease (CVD) and CVD-related mortality. A secondary analysis of The Sleep Heart Health Study (SHHS) and Multi-Ethnic Study of Atherosclerosis (MESA). High SS% and CREI were defined as the highest quartile. Lasso regression and restricted cubic spline assessed the relationship between SS%, CREI and CVD, CVD-mortality and all-cause mortality. A cumulative incidence function and a Fine-Gray subdistribution hazard model were used to evaluate this outcome accounting for competing risks. In adjusted models with age as a categorical variable divided by 65 years old, the highest quartile of SS% (HR 1.693, p: 0.017 in MESA and HR 1.240, p : 0.009 in SHHS) was associated with the incidence of CVD and was more prominent in males. A positive relationship between SS% (MESA: HR 1.429, p: 0.039; SHHS HR1.176, p:0.018 ) for the continuous metrics and CVD mortality in both cohorts was more apparent in men than in women. The categorical high-exposure association with CVD mortality was not consistent across cohorts.The associations were significantly attenuated when adjusted by age as a continuous metric. An endotype of sleep apnea reflecting high loop gain is associated with CVD and CVD mortality, especially in males.

The protocol also includes procedures to verify that ex vivo rhythms reflect the endogenous in vivo circadian phase. For complete details on the execution of this protocol, please refer to Magaña et al.1.

papers.title: Diagnostic value of extending outpatient EEG to record sleep - A retrospective study.
papers.abstract: Evidence for the utility of sleep electroencephalography (EEG) in the diagnosis of epilepsy is inconsistent, often necessitating repeat visits and sleep deprivation (SD), which increases patient and resource burden. In our setting in India, patients are often referred for EEG immediately following consultation (single visit) and EEG sessions are extended to allow for spontaneous sleep acquisition without prior SD. We aimed to evaluate the success rate of achieving sleep during these extended outpatient recordings and its incremental diagnostic yield for interictal epileptiform discharges (IEDs). We retrospectively analyzed 1762 outpatient EEGs from patients (45% female) with suspected or known epilepsy. All patients underwent an extended routine EEG (~40-50 min), incorporating standard activation procedures and aiming to capture spontaneous sleep where possible. Successful sleep acquisition was defined as the attainment of at least NREM stage N2. IED detection rates were compared between wakefulness and sleep across different epilepsy types. Sleep was achieved in 70.5% of patients (median age, 28 years; IQR: 16-55; range, 0.3-90). The proportion attaining sleep increased with recording duration, from 36.7% at 20 min to 55.6% at 30 min and 66.7% at 50 min, with a median time to sleep onset of 20 min. Among 1199 patients with both awake and sleep states captured, wakefulness identified IEDs in 29% (n = 350), while sleep captured unique IEDs in an additional 12% (n = 141), increasing the total yield significantly. In a sub-analysis of confirmed epilepsy cases (n = 751), wakefulness showed IEDs in 42% (n = 315), with sleep adding another 16% (n = 123). The diagnostic yield of sleep recordings was significantly higher than that of wakefulness alone (OR: 1.31; 95% CI: 1.02-1.68; p = 0.043), particularly among adults with idiopathic generalized epilepsy (IGE) (OR: 2.20; 95% CI: 1.30-3.73; p = 0.004) and children with self-limited epilepsy (OR: ∞; p = 0.031). Despite a busy outpatient setting, 70.5% of patients attained N2 sleep during an extended EEG recording without SD. Sleep capture increased progressively with recording duration, with the greatest incremental gain between 20 and 30 min, suggesting that a modest extension beyond 20 min substantially increases the likelihood of capturing sleep. Sleep recording increased IED detection over wakefulness alone, particularly in children, in adults with IGE, and in self-limited epilepsies. Whether this approach can substitute for a sleep-deprived EEG requires prospective, head-to-head evaluation.

papers.title: The relevance of sleep and chronopsychology in understanding maladaptive behaviors in eating disorders: A narrative review.
papers.abstract: Circadian disruption and sleep-wake dysregulation have been increasingly linked to psychiatric conditions, yet their role in eating disorders and addiction-like maladaptive behaviors remains insufficiently examined in an integrative framework. This narrative review synthesizes evidence on chronotype, circadian misalignment, sleep features, and behavioral addictions across anorexia nervosa, bulimia nervosa, orthorexic tendencies, and night eating syndrome. Literature published between 1970 and 2025 was identified through PubMed, Google Scholar, and reference screening, focusing on chronobiological, sleep-related, neuroendocrine, and behavioral aspects of eating disorders. Delayed sleep timing, eveningness preference, and insomnia symptoms commonly co-occur with disordered eating. Findings suggest overlapping mechanisms linking circadian dysregulation, sleep-related and compulsive, reward-driven behaviors, including binge eating and compensatory practices. Objective measures indicate alterations in sleep continuity, slow-wave sleep, and REM parameters. Neuroendocrine evidence further supports links among biological rhythms, appetite regulation, and sleep regulation. Preliminary chronotherapeutic interventions, such as light exposure and sleep phase modification, show promise but remain insufficiently tested. Overall, subclinical, clinical and emerging eating disorders remain underrepresented in chronobiological research. Circadian misalignment may represent a clinically relevant and modifiable dimension underlying maladaptive eating behaviors. However, fragmented evidence and methodological limitations restrict firm conclusions. A structured research agenda is proposed to guide future integrative research.

papers.title: Weighted co-expression reveals early circadian and metabolic dysregulation in precystic kidneys.
papers.abstract: Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD) initiates long before cysts appear, yet the molecular triggers of this precystic phase remain poorly defined. To gain more insight into these early alterations, we applied cross-species Weighted Gene Coexpression Network Analysis (WGCNA) to renal transcriptomes from inducible Pkd1-knockout (iKsp-Pkd1del) mice across precystic and cystic stages. Instead of constructing a new network, expression profiles were projected onto three hundred and forty-seven curated rat kidney co-expression modules from the TXG-MAPr framework, enabling direct systems-level comparison with conserved injury signatures. Forty-two transcriptionally active modules emerged, including twenty-one already deregulated during the morphologically normal precystic phase. Early upregulated modules showed activation of circadian regulators (Bmal1/Arntl, Per1, Per3, Npas2) and sterol biosynthesis under Srebf2 control, whereas mitochondrial and oxidative-phosphorylation modules were markedly repressed. Transcription-factor enrichment revealed distinct regulatory axes: circadian control by BMAL1, metabolic regulation through SREBP2 (encoded by Srebf2), and inflammatory/cytokine signaling mediated by STAT3, p53, and NF-κB. These regulatory programs diverged transcriptionally within two weeks of Pkd1 loss, establishing an epithelial-driven phase characterized by circadian misalignment, metabolic rewiring, mitochondrial suppression and concomitant low-level inflammatory signaling. Inflammatory and stress-response modules intensified during later cystic stages. Notably, Pkd2 clustered within a small but transcriptionally active high-ranked module suggesting early perturbation of the polycystin complex. Together, these data define precystic ADPKD as a convergence of independent epithelial programs accompanied by early inflammatory engagement that precedes overt cyst expansion, providing a modular framework for early biomarker discovery and therapeutic targeting.

papers.title: The Effects of Environmental Enrichment on the Behavior of Laboratory Zebrafish (Danio rerio).
papers.abstract: Enclosures for laboratory animals are often simple for economic and practical reasons. Enrichment items, such as plants, toys, and refuges, have been shown to improve measures of welfare in commonly used species such as mice and dogs. The numbers of laboratory zebrafish have been increasing in recent years, and most are housed in systems devoid of enrichment. The aim of this study is to assess the impact of environmental enrichment on adult laboratory zebrafish behavior. Experimental fish were raised in the presence of three different enrichment regimes: plastic plants, toys, and photos of gravel. These were compared to a control group raised under standard housing conditions. Once the fish reached sexual maturity, we measured aggression, reproduction, and growth. We found that each enrichment treatment led to significant reductions in aggression in a mirror test compared to control. Reproduction was largely unaffected by the three enrichment treatments. However, we found egg production was decreased following the gravel treatment, and egg survival was increased following the plant treatment. There were no significant impacts of enrichment on measures of growth. In a parallel experiment, breeding fish were exposed to plastic plant enrichment during overnight breeding. Surprisingly, there was no significant impact on egg production or egg survival.

papers.title: GraTED: Graph--Tensor EEG Decoding for Passenger Hazard Perception in Autonomous Vehicles
papers.abstract: Passenger electroencephalography (EEG) can reveal road risk through anticipatory responses before hazardous events and neural reactions around their onset. However, existing EEG decoding methods often map physiologically meaningful arrangement of electrodes onto artificial 2D grids and thus flatten the higher-order time-feature representations into matrices, obscuring meaningful structure in the data. To preserve and exploit the spatial and time-feature structure of EEG recordings, we propose the Graph-Tensor EEG Decoding Model (GraTED) for passenger risk prediction (RP) and danger identification (DI) in autonomous-vehicle scenarios. GraTED models the electrode arrangement as an undirected graph based on their scalp locations, using graph convolution to capture spatial dependencies and low-rank tensor classification to preserve the multidimensional time-feature structure, while controlling model complexity. Evaluated on the PassengerEEG dataset, comprising 11 participants and 45 hours of recordings, GraTED achieves the highest balanced accuracy, compared to the state-of-the-art, across all three evaluation settings, while requiring the fewest learnable parameters among seven baseline methods.

papers.title: Supporting the driver's perception cognition action loop using an embodied intelligent cockpit framework for explainable fatigue intervention.
papers.abstract: This study evaluated a driver-support framework combining multimodal fatigue detection, feature attribution, and state-specific auditory feedback during conditional automated driving. A fixed detector used electroencephalography (EEG), eye tracking, and vehicle dynamics. Shapley additive explanations (SHAP) selected a dominant cue, which a large language model translated into a spoken message. Fatigue labels were based on the Karolinska Sleepiness Scale and a 60-s vigilance task. Braking reaction time, standard deviation of lane position (SDLP), and time-to-collision (TTC) exposure were assessed during manual driving following takeover. Compared with generic speech, explanatory speech was associated with a 0.192-s shorter mean braking reaction time (95% confidence interval: -0.223 to -0.161 s; Holm-adjusted p < 0.001) and a 0.085-m lower mean SDLP (95% confidence interval: -0.108 to -0.062 m; Holm-adjusted p < 0.001). Further studies should separate message content from acoustic properties and assess performance in independent driving settings.

papers.title: BMAL1-Sleep interactions modulate quality of life in allergic rhinitis patients with circadian dysregulation.
papers.abstract: Circadian CLOCK genes regulate sleep and circadian rhythms. Allergic rhinitis (AR) is frequently associated with sleep disturbances that can substantially impair patient quality of life (QoL). However, the relationship between circadian CLOCK gene expression in AR and sleep-related outcomes or QoL has not been established. This study included 133 participants (100 patients with AR and 33 healthy controls). Participants completed the Morningness-Eveningness Questionnaire (MEQ), Rhinoconjunctivitis Quality of Life Questionnaire (RQLQ), and Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI). Circadian CLOCK gene expression in peripheral blood leukocytes was measured using qRT-PCR. The Mann-Whitney U test was used to compare the two independent groups and categorical variables were analyzed using the chi-square test. Linear regression evaluated the associations between circadian CLOCK gene expression and the RQLQ or sleep parameters. Patients with AR demonstrated significantly poorer sleep quality, longer sleep latency, more frequent nocturnal awakenings, and a higher prevalence of evening-type chronotypes along with dysregulated circadian gene expression in peripheral leukocytes compared to controls. Specifically, CLOCK and PER1 were upregulated and BMAL1 and CRY1 were downregulated. CLOCK expression was positively correlated with PSQI scores and negatively correlated with sleep duration in patients with AR, whereas PER2, CRY1, and CRY2 were positively correlated with sleep duration. BMAL1 expression was positively correlated with the total RQLQ score, activity limitations, and nasal symptoms. Furthermore, BMAL1 exhibited significant interactions with sleep duration on activity limitations and with sleep efficiency on nasal symptoms. Patients with AR exhibit circadian dysregulation, including imbalanced CLOCK genes, poor sleep, and evening chronotypes. The BMAL1-sleep interaction significantly influences the quality of life. Clinically, targeting this axis through interventions, such as sleep hygiene or chronotherapy, can enhance nasal symptoms and daily functioning beyond the benefits of conventional care.

papers.title: Neural and behavioral signatures of live and video demonstrations in bimanual interpersonal coordination: An EEG and kinematic study.
papers.abstract: Neural oscillations in the mu (8-12 Hz) and high-beta (21-30 Hz) bands are established markers of interpersonal coordination. During practice following the pre-test, participants trained coordinately with the model for 30 min. EEG activity was recorded from C3, Cz, and C4 electrodes, and spectral power was analyzed in the mu (8-12 Hz) and high-beta (21-30 Hz) bands. Kinematic coordination was quantified using vector coding of coupling angles between the participant and the model during execution. Results indicated significant desynchronization in both mu and high-beta bands during execution trials. Compared with the video-model condition, live-model interaction produced stronger high-beta suppression and more stable kinematic coupling. Additionally, mu suppression during observation increased across practice phases from pre-test to post-test and retention. papers.title: Intraoperative electroencephalography burst suppression during endoscopic third ventriculostomy: Case report and implications for neuromonitoring.
papers.abstract: Endoscopic third ventriculostomy (ETV) is a common treatment for obstructive hydrocephalus. Intraoperative hemodynamic disturbances are well recognized. Their concurrent association with cortical suppression on electroencephalography (EEG), particularly burst suppression, has rarely been reported, and intraoperative EEG is seldom used during ETV. A 28-year-old woman underwent ETV for obstructive hydrocephalus secondary to a tectal glioma. Shortly after endoscope insertion and ventricular irrigation, she developed two successive episodes of severe tachycardia and an acute hypertensive crisis, each coinciding with an abrupt bilateral fall in fronto-temporal electrocortical activity with burst suppression on two-channel processed EEG. Irrigation was stopped and the endoscope was withdrawn. Systemic hemodynamics normalized within 15 min, whereas the EEG required 55 min to recover. The patient recovered to near-baseline within 4 h. This report represents only the second published case coupling an acute intraoperative hemodynamic surge with bilateral EEG burst suppression during ETV. Processed intraoperative EEG may be an additional early sign of an acute disturbance of cerebral function. Its added value remains unproven, since a hemodynamic emergency already mandates cessation of irrigation and endoscope withdrawal. Prospective evaluation with finer temporal sampling and raw-EEG recording is warranted.

papers.title: Probable Rapid Eye Movement Sleep Behavior Disorder Associated With Escitalopram in a Patient With Schizoaffective Disorder: A Case Report.

Serotonergic antidepressants such as selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) are a recognized trigger, but in psychiatric patients the nocturnal behaviors are easily attributed to stress or to the primary illness. We report the case of a 46-year-old man with schizoaffective disorder, depressive type, maintained on aripiprazole 15 mg daily, who was started on escitalopram 10 mg at bedtime (day one); the dose was reduced to 5 mg on day 77. Around day 430, about 14 months after starting escitalopram and while taking 5 mg, he began to walk in his sleep and act out his dreams, including punching movements and, on one occasion, walking while holding a clothing iron, with no recollection on waking. The episodes occurred late in the night, with his eyes closed, two to three times a month and were accompanied by sleep paralysis and daytime sleepiness. His mental status examination and routine blood tests were unremarkable. He declined polysomnography and brain imaging, so a diagnosis of probable RBD, possibly associated with escitalopram, was made on clinical grounds; a non-REM parasomnia could not be excluded. On day 616, escitalopram was stopped and clonazepam 0.5 mg at bedtime was started at the same time. The episodes had stopped by day 665. Clonazepam was discontinued on day 772, and at the latest follow-up on day 1962 there had been no recurrence. Because clonazepam was started when escitalopram was withdrawn, the improvement cannot be attributed to stopping escitalopram alone, although the absence of recurrence after clonazepam was discontinued supports a role for the antidepressant. Clinicians who prescribe serotonergic antidepressants should take a sleep history from patients and their bed partners, arrange polysomnography where it is available, and review the suspected drug.

papers.title: In-person UCLA-PEERS® program for adolescents with autism spectrum disorder in Italy: study protocol for a pilot and feasibility randomized controlled trial with pragmatic features and exploratory EEG markers of treatment response.
papers.abstract: Adolescents with Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) Level 1 frequently experience persistent difficulties in peer relationships and social functioning that become more evident as social demands increase. Group-based social skills trainings represent a key evidence-based intervention for this population, yet its availability in routine clinical services is still limited. The Program for the Education and Enrichment of Relational Skills (PEERS®) is one of the most empirically supported interventions for autistic adolescents. In Italy, telemedicine delivery has shown promising results, but the effectiveness and implementation of the in-person format in real-world services have not yet been evaluated. In addition, predictors of individual response to psychosocial interventions remain largely unknown. This study is designed as a two-arm pilot and feasibility randomized controlled trial incorporating pragmatic features, including delivery within a routine tertiary clinical service, comparison with Treatment as Usual (TAU), and allowance for ongoing concomitant clinical, educational, and pharmacological treatments. It will compare the in-person Italian adaptation of UCLA PEERS® with Treatment as Usual (TAU) at IRCCS Fondazione Stella Maris (Pisa, Italy). Thirty-six adolescents aged 11-13 years with ASD (DSM-5-TR) and Full-Scale IQ >85 will be assessed at baseline (T0) and after the 16-week intervention (T1). Randomization will use block allocation with allocation concealment until completion of baseline assessments; outcome assessors and independent ADOS-BOSCC video coders will remain blind to group assignment. The intervention includes sixteen weekly 90-minute group sessions delivered by certified providers, with parallel caregiver sessions and structured teacher contacts to promote generalization. The primary focus of this pilot trial is feasibility, assessed through recruitment, retention, session attendance, and treatment fidelity. Clinical outcomes will be examined exploratorily to provide preliminary estimates of treatment effects. The QSQ-R will serve as the prespecified principal clinical outcome for estimating change in social functioning from baseline to T1. Parent- and adolescent-report versions will be analyzed separately, considering the Social Initiative and Social Reciprocity dimensions as distinct outcomes rather than deriving a composite total score. Key secondary outcomes include social knowledge (TASSK-R), autism-related social responsiveness (SRS-2), social motivation (SSDS), social anxiety (SAS), and observational change in social-communication behaviors (ADOS-BOSCC). Emotional-behavioral functioning (CBCL; YSR) will be explored as additional secondary outcomes. Baseline electroencephalography (EEG) recorded during a gesture-word integration task will be used to derive the N400 congruency effect and to explore whether individual differences in this measure are associated with treatment response. As a pilot and feasibility trial, the study is not powered for definitive efficacy testing and will estimate feasibility, acceptability, fidelity, and preliminary effect sizes to inform future multicenter trials. This study will provide the first evaluation of in-person PEERS® in the Italian clinical context and test the generalizability of previous telemedicine findings in routine care. The integration of clinical and behavioral outcomes may contribute to mechanism-informed, personalized psychosocial interventions for autistic adolescents and guide the design of future confirmatory studies. papers.title: Immunometabolic reprogramming: a working framework for disease development, endotype differentiation, and therapeutic considerations in pediatric asthma.
papers.abstract: Paediatric asthma exhibits marked clinical heterogeneity and cannot be simply considered the childhood counterpart of adult asthma. Early-life environmental exposures can reshape immune-cell metabolic programs and potentially drive long-lasting inflammatory phenotypes. Existing explanatory frameworks for paediatric asthma largely centre on Th2-related inflammation, epithelial-alarm signalling and neuro-immune crosstalk, while the contributions of immunometabolic processes to disease endotypes remain under-summarised. This review collates available evidence regarding metabolic reprogramming in the pathogenesis of paediatric asthma and provides an integrated immunometabolic perspective on this condition. Summarized evidence covers immunometabolic changes across key airway-resident and infiltrating cell populations. Discussion addresses core paediatric-specific biological features, including early-life developmental windows, virus-related trained immunity, obese asthma, circadian-sleep interactions, neuro-metabolic-immune communication and metabolomics-based endotyping. The framework is organized around substrate competition rather than a glycolysis-versus-OXPHOS binary, because Tregs, M2-like macrophages and pathogenic ILC2s share lipid and amino-acid pools but exert opposing functions. From these observations emerges a testable "Metabolic Latching Model" of how early-life insults establish persistent inflammatory memory through metabolism-epigenetic coupling, with "latching" operationally defined by exposure removal and persistence beyond responding-cell turnover. Group 2 innate lymphoid cells (ILC2s) and the Treg-to-effector balance are placed at the centre of this framework. Three hypotheses are prioritised as feasible with current technology: H1 (monocyte glycolytic baseline predicting wheeze-to-asthma transition), H4 (metabolic intervention in obese asthma), and H6 (the HDAC2-GSH/butyrate axis in steroid sensitivity). Current evidence suggests that immunometabolic reprogramming serves as one plausible contributing factor for the heterogeneity of paediatric asthma. This conceptual framework may bridge molecular metabolic findings and paediatric clinical contexts, and inform future mechanistic and clinical studies in this research area.

papers.title: Noise Pollution in Cement Manufacturing Industries: A Comprehensive Review of Environmental and Occupational Health Impacts and Mitigation Strategies.
papers.abstract: The process of cement production is a somewhat neglected yet considerable contributor to noise pollution both in the workplace and its surroundings, as it produces high-intensity noise through various activities such as crushing, grinding, and heating. In the paper that follows, recent literature concerning the sources and effects of noise pollution in cement production is analyzed, and the effectiveness of various noise mitigation strategies is assessed. Publications from 2015 to 2025 were reviewed, along with some prior publications, focusing on various noise sources, effects on workers and the environment, and noise mitigation strategies. Loudness in cement-producing plants is about 68.8-103.3 dB(A) and is continuous in nature, unlike other industries' processes, which are characterized by sound bursts only. Subsequent effects on job-related experiences and workers' functioning include negative effects on hearing ability, heart problems, sleep disorders, and stress, which increases considerably due to the mixture of loudness with dust and chemicals; noise impacts animals' behavior, communication, and habitat. Together, engineering controls, administrative controls, and spatial planning in facilities form a structured control hierarchy that has proven to be effective. However, its implementation is hampered by high cost and inconsistent regulation across regions of the world. Most of the evidence for the reliability of this approach comes from cross-sectional studies of single factories with scarce longitudinal data. Hence, noise pollution in the cement production process presents a major multi-faceted risk for employees, and to mitigate this risk effectively, coordinated engineering, administrative, and regulatory measures must be applied.

papers.title: Rivastigmine and Emerging Nanotechnological Strategies for Targeted Delivery: A Comprehensive Review.
papers.abstract: Alzheimer's disease affects millions of people globally; it is an irreversible and incurable disease, characterized by gradual cognitive decline as well as pathophysiological changes including the presence of senile plaques and neurofibrillary tangles. There are several risk factors associated with Alzheimer's disease, including elevated blood pressure, blood sugar concentration, alcohol consumption, smoking, and sleep disturbances. Rivastigmine is an FDA-approved cholinesterase inhibitor used to treat Alzheimer's disease. It is available as oral solutions, capsules, and transdermal patches. Oral administration can lead to detrimental and off-target effects such as nausea and vomiting, and the use of patches can cause irritation and rashes. Across various systems, including the Cardiovascular (CVS), Gastrointestinal (GI), immunological, dermatological, and respiratory systems, rivastigmine has been associated with effects that further necessitate targeted drug delivery. Novel drug delivery systems such as Liposomes, Polymeric Nanoparticles, Dendrimers, Solid Lipid Nanoparticles (SLNs), Nanostructured Lipid Carriers (NLCs), nano-emulsions, and Mesoporous Silica Nanoparticles (MSNs) have been developed to address the limitations of conventional dosage forms. These new formulations possess the ability to increase drug loading capacity, enhance penetration across the BBB, reduce expulsion, and offer controlled release of the drug. As a result, rivastigmine can be targeted to the intended site, with fewer off-target effects. However, formulation-specific toxicity may still occur. Positive off-target effects, such as improved appetite, protection against malnutrition, and evidence of advantage in treating colitis, were also observed with rivastigmine. However, detailed studies of its mechanism of action are needed to provide a scientifically sound justification for repurposing rivastigmine. Google Scholar and PubMed were searched for literature for this review and included studies that met the criteria.

papers.title: The quiet end of the spectrum: A case report and review of "simple schizophrenia".
papers.abstract: BackgroundSchizophrenia is increasingly understood as a neurodevelopmental disorder in which cognitive and negative symptoms may precede or overshadow florid psychosis. Such neuropsychiatric presentations can be difficult to recognise within current diagnostic frameworks that privilege positive symptoms.ObjectiveTo illustrate a schizophrenia presentation without hallucinations and delusions and to contextualise it within contemporary and historical nosology.MethodsSingle case report with a focussed narrative review of the literature on simple schizophrenia subtypes.Casea 24-year-old woman experienced a two-year insidious decline in motivation, social engagement, and cognition, with prominent affective flattening, avolition, bradyphrenia, poverty of speech, and psychomotor slowing. There were no delusions or hallucinations, and thought form was linear. Extensive investigations including MRI, EEG, FDG-PET, and CSF studies were unremarkable. Neuropsychological testing showed deficits in new learning, processing speed, and executive functioning consistent with schizophrenia-spectrum illness. The illness was refractory to multiple antidepressants, antipsychotics, and a course of electroconvulsive therapy. Following exclusion of organic pathology, multidisciplinary assessment, and longitudinal review, a diagnosis of schizophrenia was formulated.ConclusionCurrent diagnostic systems may overlook individuals with schizophrenia without hallucinations or delusions. Incorporating neuropsychiatric markers and establishing cognitive trajectories into diagnostic thinking may enable earlier identification and more targeted interventions.

papers.title: Sphenoidal Meningioma with Focal Seizures Masquerading as Immune Reconstitution Inflammatory Syndrome in HIV Patient.
papers.abstract: Seizures in adults with HIV can result from structural lesions, opportunistic infections, immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (IRIS) or medication effects, making accurate diagnosis challenging. We report a 47-year-old woman with HIV who developed recurrent focal-onset seizures evolving to bilateral tonic-clonic seizures beginning approximately 4 weeks after initiation of antiretroviral therapy (ART). Neurological examination was unremarkable. Electroencephalography revealed focal slowing over the left anterior temporal region without generalised epileptiform discharges. Targeted infectious testing, including Toxoplasma gondii , Cryptococcus neoformans and Mycobacterium tuberculosis , was negative. Brain magnetic resonance imaging performed at the time of evaluation demonstrated a well-circumscribed, extra-axial mass over the left sphenoid wing measuring 3.0 cm × 4.3 cm, isointense on T1-and T2-weighted sequences, with vasogenic oedema and midline shift, consistent with meningioma. Seizure control was achieved with antiseizure medication; however, definitive treatment required gross total surgical resection. Following surgery, the patient remained seizure-free at 12 months of follow-up. Although ART initiation initially suggested central nervous system IRIS, preserved immune function, negative infectious workup and characteristic imaging confirmed a structural aetiology. This case highlights the importance of a broad differential diagnosis and integrating clinical, electrophysiological, infectious and imaging data to identify treatable structural lesions in adults with HIV.

papers.title: Revamped transposon-induced hepatocellular carcinoma model reveals deep similarities of cancer-driver landscapes across mice and humans
papers.abstract: Genome-scale cancer-driver discovery is limited by statistical uncertainty in driver calling and by experimental constraints on mutations available for selection. We developed 3xfOnc3 - a three-frame Sleeping Beauty (SB) mutagenesis system designed to broaden functional perturbations and reduce integration biases of traditional SB screens - and tested it in vivo in mouse liver. Within 12 months, 60% of mice developed heterogeneous hepatocellular tumors. Tumor-selected integrations were interpreted against an empirical reference from SB-based therapeutic gene delivery to hepatocytes, enabling correction for gene targetability. Background-aware filtering prioritized 315 driver candidates, including 243 protein-coding genes. Tumors were multiclonal, and identical integration-marked lineages expanded differently across lesions, supporting context-dependent clonal expansion. SB hits within young L1 subfamily members were selectively enriched in tumors. Human orthologues of candidate drivers were enriched for Cancer Gene Census genes and protein-altering pan-cancer mutations. Together, 3xfOnc3 reveals a background-corrected driver landscape linking driver selection to clonal tumor evolution and cross-species cancer relevance.

papers.title: An integrative view of human nociceptor diversity: from microneurography to molecular identity.
papers.abstract: Neuropathic pain arises from dysfunction of the peripheral or central nervous system and affects up to 10% of the population worldwide. Aberrant activity in injured sensory nerve fibers, particularly spontaneous firing and altered conduction properties of nociceptors, is tightly linked to pain, yet its molecular underpinnings in humans have long remained elusive. Over recent years, major technological advances have transformed both functional and molecular analyses of sensory neurons. High-resolution single-cell and spatial transcriptomics have produced detailed atlases of sensory neuron diversity, while traditional electrophysiological approaches such as patch-clamp and microneurography have provided unparalleled insight into nerve fiber properties. Despite their individual strengths, molecular and functional classifications of sensory neurons have largely evolved in parallel. This review focuses on emerging strategies that bridge these approaches to achieve an integrated, mechanistic understanding of neuropathic pain. We discuss how microneurography-defined biophysical hallmarks, such as activity-dependent slowing, recovery cycle signatures, and following frequency, can be transferred into in vitro patch-clamp paradigms, enabling direct functional comparison with dissociated human and large-animal sensory neurons. The incorporation of Patch-seq approaches has further enabled the assignment of molecular identity to functionally defined nociceptor subtypes, exemplified by the characterization of the mechano-insensitive "sleeping" nociceptors. Finally, we highlight how multimodal datasets combining electrophysiology, transcriptomics, and computational modeling provide new opportunities to unravel the ion channel mechanisms, particularly sodium channel subtypes, that shape pathological firing states. By directly linking human nerve fiber function to molecular programs, this integrative framework paves the way toward stratified, mechanism-based therapies for neuropathic pain.
